# Title:Quantitative stability of optimal transport via regularization

Authors:Songbo Wang, Xiaozhen Wang

View a PDF of the paper titled Quantitative stability of optimal transport via regularization, by Songbo Wang and Xiaozhen Wang

View PDF HTML (experimental)

> Abstract:We prove quantitative stability estimates for quadratic optimal transport maps by regularizing a Brenier potential and estimating the error in the duality gap. The source has an $L^p$ density, $p>1$, relative to a probability measure with a BV density. When one target lies in a fixed ball, we obtain the $W_2$ Hölder exponent $(p-1)/(4p-2)$. The constant depends on the dimension through three explicit source quantities: the variance, the total variation of the reference density and the $L^p$ norm of the weight. The proof uses a second-order bound on the averaged regularized Fenchel gap. By restricting the slopes of the potential, we also treat targets with a bounded moment of any order greater than two. In both estimates, the condition is imposed on one target, while the other can be any probability measure with finite second moment. For Gaussian and isotropic log-concave sources, the constants grow polynomially with the dimension. For $L^p$ changes of Gaussian measure, the factor in the bounded-target estimate is $d^{(p-1)/(4p-2)}$. For each $p$, a fixed source in two dimensions proves optimality of both stability exponents in this source class. A Gaussian construction provides polynomial lower bounds on the dimension dependence.

## 🏷️ The proposed matching upper bound

For finite targets, a convex potential is a maximum of affine functions; its cells have prescribed masses. Moving intercepts changes both cell masses and first moments. The manuscript’s central estimate controls the squared first-moment derivatives, weighted by inverse cell masses, by the similarly weighted mass derivatives, uniformly through cell degeneration.

Along a transport of target sites, the mass constraints give a graph-Laplacian equation for intercept velocities. The moment estimate controls the needed velocities without a uniform bound for the inverse graph Laplacian. After fixing the additive constants of the potentials, this produces an L 2 potential difference of order W 2​.

A convex-gradient interpolation estimate then has the form

∥∇u−∇v∥2 2​≤C(h−2∥u−v∥2 2​+h).​

Balancing terms with h=W 2 2/3​ gives a squared-gradient bound of order W 2 2/3​ and hence the one-third exponent. Approximation extends the finite-target result to arbitrary compactly supported targets. The uniform moment estimate is the main new input; the balancing calculation alone does not establish it.

## 🏷️ Key steps and proof outlines

### The crucial estimate concerns cell moments, not site separation

For a finite target, write the convex potential as u(x)=max i​{x⋅y i​+c i​}. Its cells P i​ are the regions where the i th affine function wins. Let M i​=ρ(P i​) and B i​=∫P i​​x d ρ. Varying the intercepts in a direction q while keeping the sites fixed gives the source’s central estimate

i∑​M i​∣D B i​[q]∣2​≤162 R 2 i∑​M i​∣D M i​[q]∣2​,

where K⊂B(0,R) and ρ is normalized volume on K. The bound is uniform even when some masses or site separations are tiny.

Proof outline. Compare the cells at c−s q and c+s q. Couple their uniform laws by the same successive conditional quantiles. The midpoint of the coupled points belongs to the original cell: averaging the two affine cell inequalities cancels the intercept perturbation. The triangular quantile maps have products of diagonal derivatives equal to their cell volumes. Arithmetic–geometric mean applied to those derivatives bounds the midpoint density by the inverse geometric mean of the two volumes.

Now use Φ(x)=R 2−∣x∣2≥0 and its exact midpoint identity

Φ(2 X+Z​)=2 Φ(X)+Φ(Z)​+4∣X−Z∣2​.

Summing over cells cancels the endpoint partition integrals. If α i​,β i​ are the two masses and γ i​=α i​β i​​, the remaining estimate controls ∑i​γ i​E∣X i​−Z i​∣2 by 5 R 2∑i​(α i​−β i​)2/γ i​. First moments differ by a mass-change term plus a displacement term. Cauchy–Schwarz bounds both; division by (2 s)2 and passage to the derivative limit give the displayed constant. The allowed size of s may depend on the configuration, but the resulting derivative constant does not. (OpenAI, 2026)

### Moving sites while holding their transported masses fixed

Take an optimal finite coupling ∑i​m i​δ(y i 0​,y i 1​)​ between the targets and interpolate y i​(t)=(1−t)y i 0​+t y i 1​. Put v i​=y i 1​−y i 0​ and w=W 2​(μ,ν), so ∑i​m i​∣v i​∣2=w 2. Pairwise optimality gives (y i 0​−y j 0​)⋅(y i 1​−y j 1​)≥0; hence distinct endpoint pairs produce distinct sites at every interior time.

Choose intercepts so the cell masses remain m i​, normalized by ∑i​m i​c i​(t)=0. Their derivatives r i​=c i′​(t) have weighted mean zero. The cell-mass derivative matrix is a connected weighted graph Laplacian, so an intercept direction q can be chosen with D M i​[q]=m i​r i​. Differentiating the fixed-mass constraints and using symmetry of face contributions yields

i∑​m i​r i 2​=−i∑​v i​⋅D B i​[q].

Weighted Cauchy–Schwarz and the moment estimate give

(i∑​m i​r i 2​)1/2≤162​Rw.

No bound on q itself is required. Since ∂t​u t​=x⋅v i​+r i​ on cell i, integration in time proves ∥u 1​−u 0​∥L 2(ρ)​≤(1+162​)Rw. This is the stable quantity before taking gradients. (OpenAI, 2026)

### Why differentiation changes a linear estimate into a one-third estimate

On each coordinate interval of the convex body, a convex L-Lipschitz function has a monotone derivative bounded by L. Its forward difference quotient differs from that derivative by a nonnegative quantity whose integral is at most 2 L h: the interior translated integrals cancel, leaving two endpoint intervals of length h. Squaring costs another factor 2 L. The excluded boundary portions also have total volume bounded by h times the coordinate projection area.

Summing these slice estimates gives, for f=u 0​−u 1​,

∥∇u 0​−∇u 1​∥2 2​≤h 2 12 d​∥f∥2 2​+∣K∣28 L 2 P K​​h,

where P K​ is the sum of coordinate projection volumes. Substituting ∥f∥2​=O(w) and choosing h=w 2/3 balances the two terms at order w 2/3. Taking square roots yields the exponent 1/3.

Finally, approximate arbitrary compactly supported targets by finite nets. The uniform estimate makes their maps Cauchy in L 2. Uniform limits of normalized convex potentials provide supporting inequalities for the limit map; the Fenchel equality identifies it as the unique optimal map. Thus no lower target-density bound or uniform atom separation is introduced in the limiting argument. (OpenAI, 2026)
